content: 1. Integrated HIV services are less stigmatizing compared to stand-alone care models, as demonstrated in a comparative case study conducted in Swaziland and published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society in 2013. 2. A systematic review published in BMJ Open in 2017 highlights the integration of sexually transmitted infection (STI) services into HIV care and treatment services for women living with HIV, emphasizing its potential benefits. 3. A systematic review in the journal Sexually Transmitted Infections (2012) analyzed the costs and efficiency of integrating HIV/AIDS services with other health services, providing evidence and experiences from various settings. 4. The integration of HIV and tuberculosis (TB) services in sub-Saharan Africa was systematically reviewed in The Lancet Infectious Diseases (2011), demonstrating the importance of combined service delivery in high-burden regions. 5. A systematic review published in AIDS Care (2017) evaluated whether trained lay providers should perform HIV testing, providing evidence to inform World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines. 6. The WHO guideline on health policy and system support for optimizing community health worker programs, accessed in November 2019, provides a framework for improving community-based health interventions. 7. The International AIDS Society (2018) developed a decision framework for differentiated service delivery for HIV testing services, aiming to enhance accessibility and efficiency. 8. WHO's 2010 initiative, Towards universal access, outlines strategies for scaling up HIV prevention, treatment, care, and support in collaboration with countries. 9. A study published in Sexually Transmitted Infections (2016) reported high HIV incidence among men who have sex with men attending community-based voluntary counseling and testing services in Barcelona, Spain, based on findings from the ITACA cohort. 10. The implementation of couples’ voluntary HIV counseling and testing services in Durban, South Africa, was documented in BMC Public Health (2015), highlighting its feasibility and outcomes. 11. WHO's 2007 guidance on provider-initiated HIV testing and counseling in health facilities emphasizes the importance of proactive testing strategies. 12. The ECHO trial consortium (2019) investigated HIV incidence among women using different contraceptive methods, including depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, copper intrauterine devices, and levonorgestrel implants, in a randomized, multicenter trial published in The Lancet. 13. A systematic review in Reproductive Health (2019) examined the integration of HIV testing services into family planning services, emphasizing its potential to improve health outcomes. 14. The 2019 Global Tuberculosis Report by WHO provides comprehensive data on TB prevalence and its intersection with HIV, accessed in November 2019. 15. WHO's consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services (2019) offer evidence-based recommendations for improving testing strategies globally. 16. A systematic review and meta-analysis published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society (2018) revealed high HIV and active TB prevalence among adults with TB symptoms, along with increased mortality risks. 17. WHO's guidelines for intensified TB case-finding and isoniazid preventive therapy for people living with HIV in resource-constrained settings, accessed in August 2019, provide critical recommendations for TB-HIV co-management. 18. A systematic review in Sexually Transmitted Infections (2011) explored the prevalence of sexually transmitted co-infections in people living with HIV/AIDS, with implications for using HIV treatments for prevention. 19. Studies evaluating the effectiveness of opt-out HIV testing strategies in STI clinics, such as those published in Sexually Transmitted Infections (2009), demonstrate increased testing uptake and early diagnosis. 20. A controlled trial in Cape Town, South Africa, published in Implementation Science (2010), assessed the impact of provider-initiated (opt-out) HIV testing and counseling for patients with sexually transmitted infections. 21. WHO's 2019 guidelines on HIV self-testing and partner notification provide a supplement to the consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services, emphasizing innovative approaches to increase testing coverage. 22. A randomized trial in AIDS and Behavior (2018) demonstrated that HIV self-testing increases testing frequency among high-risk men who have sex with men. 23. A study in BMC Public Health (2019) evaluated the impact of announcing the availability of oral HIV self-test kits via text messages to increase testing among hard-to-reach populations, such as truck drivers in Kenya. 24. A randomized controlled trial in AIDS Care (2018) assessed the feasibility of offering self-administered oral HIV testing to truck drivers in Kenya, showing increased testing uptake. 25. The eSTAMP study (2015-2016) evaluated the impact of HIV self-testing among internet-recruited men who have sex with men, presented at the 9th IAS Conference on HIV Science in 2017. 26. A randomized clinical trial published in PLOS Medicine (2016) promoted partner and couples testing through secondary distribution of HIV self-tests, demonstrating its effectiveness in increasing testing rates. 27. A pilot study in Sexually Transmitted Infections (2018) explored the provision of home HIV self-testing kits for patients who declined testing in emergency departments, showing increased engagement in HIV testing. 28. A randomized controlled trial in AIDS and Behavior (2018) evaluated the efficacy of promoting home-based HIV self-testing with online counseling to increase testing among men who have sex with men in China. 29. A pilot randomized controlled trial in AIDS Patient Care and STDs (2018) assessed the impact of HIV self-testing and real-time post-test counseling/referral on screening and preventive care among men who have sex with men. 30. A randomized controlled trial in AIDS and Behavior (2019) evaluated the effects of a mobile health intervention to promote HIV self-testing among men who have sex with men in China, demonstrating its potential to increase testing rates.
